video.title: How She Built a 6-Figure Business Teaching People About Goats

summary: Deborah describes building a goat education business from a homesteading blog into a mix of online courses, a paid membership, books, advertising, and live experiences. She explains how search content and an email list bring in customers, and how the membership combines courses, community, and personal help. The business also earns from display ads and YouTube, while farm events and a Portugal goat tour extend the community in person. Her main lessons are to build an email list early, focus on a niche, and create useful content from real customer questions.

ideas.name: Goat and homesteading online courses

pricing.model: One-time purchase; seasonal courses were sometimes discounted.

price_points.label: Course price cited by the host

acquisition_channels.details: Articles answer common goat-owner queries, including feeding, weight, birthing, and parasites; readers can opt in for related free resources.

tools: Kit (name is unclear in the transcript)

tactics.name: Build a niche audience before pitching a product
steps: Publish practical content about a specific topic and make it easy for a relevant organization or event to discover it.
Place the blog link where the target community already looks; Deborah's blog was linked from the Mother Earth News Fair website.
Use speaking or other public appearances to demonstrate expertise.

quote.text: And there was a link to my blog on the Mother Earth News Fair website and they read it.
quote.speaker: Deborah

tactics.name: Start an email list and use a useful lead magnet
steps: Offer a practical free resource that solves a common problem, such as a goat food cheat sheet or mineral comparison chart.
Ask visitors to provide an email address to receive the resource.
Send relevant material that follows the audience's seasonal needs.

quote.text: And that's where people sign up for our email list or get one of our freebies like our goat mineral comparison chart or something like that.
quote.speaker: Deborah

tactics.name: Keep subscribers informed while building a product
steps: Tell the list what you are building and share progress as it happens.
Keep communicating if production takes longer than planned.
Open sales to an audience that has already been following the work.

quote.text: I read Jeff Walker's book and he says in there to get your audience invested in what you're creating by keeping them informed about your progress.
quote.speaker: Deborah

tactics.name: Use seasonal course promotions
steps: Choose the course that matches a seasonal customer problem.
Promote that course during the relevant month and offer a 20% discount.
Stop repeating promotions if the sales no longer justify the email volume.

quote.text: So like in January, the goat birthing course is 20% off. In April, the parasite course is 20% off because that's when you're gonna have parasite problems.
quote.speaker: Deborah

tactics.name: Turn repeated customer questions into reusable content
steps: Notice questions that would otherwise require a long email exchange.
Answer complex or broadly useful questions in a video or livestream.
Link viewers to the related articles, videos, courses, or membership resources.

quote.text: So I'm just gonna hop on YouTube and do a live stream and say, well, if this is the case, then this is what you need to do.

tactics.name: Ask the audience what format they want
steps: Survey the email list regularly about product ideas and preferred formats.
Compare interest in one-time course purchases with membership access.
Use the answers and actual sales trends to decide which offers to keep promoting.

tactics.name: Combine courses and community on one platform
steps: Put the courses and member discussions in the same place.
Make community access available at the basic membership level.
Use relevant course links to answer questions rather than rewriting the same explanation each time.

tactics.name: Measure time use before hiring
steps: Use a time-tracking tool to identify recurring work that takes too much of the founder's week.
Hire a virtual assistant for repeatable social media work.
Give the assistant clear routines for checking messages and linking people to existing resources.
Escalate complex cases to a human with the right subject expertise.
